conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. Your answers are completely confidential, and there are no right or wrong responses—only what’s true for you. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can share as much or as little as you like. Ready to begin?

In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… not very often. Maybe once or twice when my partner made a silly face at the baby, but even then the laugh felt kind of forced and faded fast. Most of the time things just don’t feel funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not much… maybe once or twice when my partner did something goofy with the baby, but the laugh felt kind of flat and disappeared right away. Mostly I just feel too tired or down to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but this past week nothing sounds all that great. I still go through the motions, hoping I’ll feel something, but the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the “right” way. When I couldn’t get him to nap yesterday I sat there crying, telling myself I’m a terrible mom. I know, logically, babies just cry, but the guilt still jumps on me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly worry that he’s not breathing right, or I’ll lie down and my mind starts racing about all the awful “what-ifs.” I check on him three, four times a night just to be sure. I know nothing’s wrong, but I can’t stop the anxious loop.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times this week. Once, I was just folding laundry and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t breathe. I knew nothing bad was happening, but my body felt like there was danger right in front of me. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky and on edge the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, trying to grab a bite myself—there’s already another mess or cry waiting. I’ll look around at the dishes or the pile of laundry and feel like I’m drowning, wondering how other moms handle it all. I still manage, but it’s this constant weight pressing on me.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… three nights this week I just stared at the ceiling for over an hour. My thoughts kept circling: "I'm failing him, tomorrow will be just as hard, I'll never feel rested again." Even when the baby was asleep, I couldn't settle. I finally dozed off, but woke again with my heart pounding and couldn't get back to sleep for ages.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days I feel like that… it’s not tears-every-second, but there’s this heavy sadness sitting on me. I’ll watch the baby smile and still feel a lump in my throat, like I’m carrying around a gray cloud I can’t shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times. Yesterday I burst into tears while trying to soothe the baby—he wouldn’t latch, I felt useless, and the tears just came. Another night I cried quietly in the shower so no one would hear. It’s not all-day sobbing, but when the pressure builds up, I can’t hold it in.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yes… maybe once or twice this week. It flashed through my mind—like “what if I just kept driving past the house and didn’t come back,” or “what if I fell asleep and didn’t wake up.” I don’t have a plan and I don’t want to leave my baby, but those quick thoughts still scared me when they showed up.

I hear how heavy everything feels right now-how joy seems out of reach, how worries crowd your mind even when your baby is peacefully asleep, and how ordinary tasks feel like climbing a mountain with no summit in sight. You're working so hard to be the mom you want to be, yet you're carrying a constant gray cloud of sadness, <sym>guilt</sym>, and <sym>anxiety</sym>. The brief flashes of wanting to disappear scare you, and the tears that sneak up leave you feeling depleted. Please know that what you're experiencing is not a personal failing; it's a signal that you need and deserve support, and reaching out today is a brave first step.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, fleeting laughter with diminished enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely not so much now".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing absence of spark despite trying to engage</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('a lot') tied to specific mothering tasks and labels herself a 'terrible mom,' matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive worries with compulsive checking and racing thoughts, aligning with 'very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple discrete panic-like episodes this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily overwhelm and difficulty managing tasks, indicating reduced coping ability but not complete inability.</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses frequent, prolonged sleep disruption directly tied to distressing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Heavy daily sadness and inability to feel joy despite baby's smile aligns with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple tearful episodes triggered by maternal stress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes passive suicidal ideation occurring once or twice this week, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with <med>peripartum onset</med>. Over the past week you report core symptoms: diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), significant self-reproach, daily <sym>anxiety</sym> with nocturnal checking, discrete panic attacks, sleep disruption not explained by infant care alone, persistent low mood, tearfulness, and passive suicidal ideation (<quote>what if I just kept driving past the house</quote>). These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for a major depressive episode. Because Q10 ≥1, immediate safety assessment is indicated. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local <med>perinatal mental health crisis line</med>
2. Develop a written safety plan that includes 24-h support numbers and removing potential means of self-harm
3. Ask your provider about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> and discuss risks/benefits of <med>sertraline</med> or similar <med>antidepressants</med> compatible with breastfeeding
4. Enlist practical help-partner, family, or postpartum doula-for night feeds and household tasks so you can secure 4-hour blocks of sleep
5. Schedule daily 20-min outdoor walks; gentle movement and morning light can modestly lift mood
6. Join a local or virtual new-mom support group to reduce isolation and normalize your experience
7. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track response to interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, 1 week post-delivery, partner present

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS-relevant):
- Anhedonia/lack of joy (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame (Q3)  
- Persistent generalized anxiety & nocturnal checking (Q4)  
- Acute panic episode (Q5)  
- Overwhelm/daily functioning strain (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)  
- Depressed mood/crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Passive suicidal ideation without plan (“kept driving… didn’t wake up”) (Q10)

Pattern: Consistent dysphoric mood, loss of pleasure, marked anxiety/panic, guilt, functional overwhelm, and safety concern.

Risk flags:
- Passive suicidal thoughts present → safety screening indicated  
- Moderate-to-severe symptom burden across emotional, cognitive, physiologic domains  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood, not solely infant care  
- No psychotic features reported; no substance use endorsed.

Screening impression: High clinical concern for Major Depressive Episode with anxious features; rule-out postpartum anxiety disorder. Recommend immediate safety plan, formal diagnostic assessment, and expedited referral to perinatal psychiatry / therapy services.
